# ClientX

> ClientX is a library for typed, declarative HTTP API clients on Python 3.12+, built on httpx2 and Pydantic v2. You declare endpoints as decorated methods with empty bodies; ClientX builds each request from the method's signature and annotations and decodes the response into the declared return type. It can also describe a client's endpoints as AI tools and serve them over MCP.

Install with `pip install clientx`, or `pip install "clientx[mcp]"` for the MCP server. ClientX depends on `httpx2`, which is a different package from `httpx`: import `httpx2`, not `httpx`.

A complete client:

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter

from clientx import Body, ClientX, DumpConfig, PathParam, Query, Resource, Response
from clientx.decoders import ModelDecoder, TypeAdapterDecoder
from clientx.methods import delete, get, patch, post


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str


class NewUser(BaseModel):
    name: str


class UserChanges(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None


class Users(Resource, prefix="/users", tags=["users"]):
    @get("/{user_id}", decoder=ModelDecoder(User))
    def retrieve(self, user_id: Annotated[int, PathParam(description="The user's ID")]) -> User:
        """Fetch one user by ID."""
        ...

    @get("", decoder=TypeAdapterDecoder(TypeAdapter(list[User])))
    def search(self, name: Annotated[str, Query("q")], limit: Annotated[int | None, Query()] = None) -> list[User]:
        """Search users by name."""
        ...

    @post("", decoder=ModelDecoder(User))
    def create(self, payload: NewUser) -> User:
        """Create a user."""
        ...

    @patch("/{user_id}", decoder=ModelDecoder(User))
    def update(
        self, user_id: int, changes: Annotated[UserChanges, Body(dump_config=DumpConfig(exclude_unset=True))]
    ) -> User:
        """Change some of a user's fields."""
        ...

    @delete("/{user_id}")
    def remove(self, user_id: int) -> None:
        """Delete a user."""
        ...


class ExampleAPI(ClientX):
    users = Users()

    @get("/health")
    def health(self) -> Response:
        """Check the service."""
        ...


# A 4xx or 5xx response raises httpx2.HTTPStatusError from any endpoint (raise_for_status=False turns it off).
with ExampleAPI("https://api.example.com", auth=("user", "secret"), timeout=10.0) as api:
    user = api.users.retrieve(42)  # GET /users/42 -> User
    matches = api.users.search("Ada")  # GET /users?q=Ada -> list[User] (limit is None, so it's left out)
    api.users.create(NewUser(name="Ada"))  # POST /users with JSON {"name": "Ada"}
    api.users.update(42, UserChanges(name="Ada L."))  # PATCH /users/42 with JSON {"name": "Ada L."}
```

Rules for writing endpoints:

- Endpoint bodies never run. Write `...` (or just a docstring). Decorators come from `clientx.methods`: `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, `head`, `options`. Each takes `path`, and optionally `decoder`, `deprecated` (for example `DeprecatedMessage("...")`), `tags`, `timeout`, and `raise_for_status` (`True`/`False`, overriding the client's).
- Every endpoint needs a return annotation. `-> Response` (`clientx.Response` is `httpx2.Response`) returns the raw response, `-> None` returns nothing, and any other type requires `decoder=`. Type checkers check that the decoder's output matches the annotation. A missing annotation or decoder raises when the class is defined.
- Decoders, from `clientx.decoders`: `ModelDecoder(Model)`, `TypeAdapterDecoder(TypeAdapter(T))` (it takes a `TypeAdapter`, not a bare type), `FromResponseDecoder(Model)` (calls `Model.from_response(response)`), `json_decoder` (returns `Any`), `text_decoder`, `content_decoder`, or any callable `(httpx2.Response) -> T`. A 4xx or 5xx response raises `httpx2.HTTPStatusError` before the decoder runs; otherwise a decoder always runs when given.
- `{placeholders}` in the path are filled from parameters with the same names, including placeholders in a resource prefix. Values are converted like query values (an `Enum` becomes its value) and percent-encoded as one segment, so `/` `?` `#` and `..` in a value can't change the path. Use `{name:path}` to keep slashes in a value such as a file path; any other converter raises `PathTemplateError`. A `None` or empty value, or a `{name:path}` value with a leading, trailing, or doubled slash, raises `PathValueError` before sending, since it would call a different path. Don't pre-encode values: `%` would be encoded again.
- Each other parameter goes to the first of these that matches: (1) its name is a request part (`params`, `json`, `data`, `files`, `headers`), which wins even over an annotation, so a parameter named `data` is always form data; (2) a request-part annotation: `Annotated[T, Query()]` (query parameters), `Header()`, `Form()` (form data), `Body()` (JSON body), or `File()` (multipart files); (3) its value is a Pydantic model, which is expanded field by field (fields annotated with a helper go to that part, the rest to the JSON body). Anything else raises `UnconsumableArgumentError`. Arguments for the same part merge in parameter order, and later ones win silently (dicts key by key; any other value replaces the part).
- `Query`, `Header`, and `Form` take an optional `key`, the name to send under: `Query("userId")`. Without it, a single value (str, int, Enum, list) is sent under the parameter name, and `Header()` turns underscores into hyphens (`request_id` becomes `request-id`). A list repeats the name (`?tag=a&tag=b`). A mapping or model is merged into the part. Model fields follow the same rules, under their alias or field name. `Body()` and `File()` take no key; on a model field they merge the value into that part, so it must be a mapping or a model, and anything else (`None` included) raises `UnconsumableArgumentError`.
- `None` is never sent as a query parameter, header, or form field, so optional parameters work as `Annotated[int | None, Query()] = None`; pass `""` to send an empty value. A JSON body keeps `null`. Values become JSON-compatible: an `Enum` its `.value`, a `datetime` ISO 8601, a `UUID` a string; numbers and booleans in headers become text.
- Models are dumped with `mode="json"` and `by_alias=True`, so fields are sent under their aliases (`Field(alias="userId")` or `alias_generator=to_camel`): don't add `serialize_by_alias`. Every helper takes `dump_config=DumpConfig(...)`, whose keys override those defaults and go to `model_dump`: `exclude_unset=True` (only the fields that were set, for PATCH), `exclude_none`, `exclude_defaults`, `include`, `exclude`, `by_alias`, `mode`, `context`, `round_trip`, `serialize_as_any`, `exclude_computed_fields`, `warnings`.
- Reuse annotations with `type` aliases: `type UserId = Annotated[int | None, Query("userId")]`. A helper applies to the whole parameter or field: one helper, in the outermost `Annotated`, around the full type with `None` inside (`Annotated[int | None, Query()]`, `QueryParam[int | None]`). A helper nested inside another type (`Annotated[int, Query()] | None`, `list[Annotated[str, Query()]]`) or a second helper raises `MisplacedHelperError`. If the part depends on the value's type, write separate endpoints.
- The helpers are named like FastAPI's but build the outgoing request. In a FastAPI app, import ClientX's under another name (`from clientx import Query as ClientQuery`) or use `clientx.Query(...)`.
- Streaming: `StreamLinesDecoder()` and `StreamChunksDecoder(chunk_size=...)` with `-> Iterator[str]` / `-> Iterator[bytes]` stream the body and release the connection when iteration ends. `StreamResponseDecoder()` with `-> Response` returns the open response, which the caller must read or close.
- Resources group endpoints: `class Users(Resource, prefix="/users", tags=[...])`, mounted as an instance (`users = Users()`) on a `ClientX` subclass or on another resource. Prefixes are absolute (they're not combined when nesting); put an API-wide prefix such as `/v1` in the base URL. Resource tags come before each endpoint's tags. Calling a resource that isn't mounted raises `UnboundResourceError`.
- An endpoint's name hides any other meaning of that name for the rest of the class body. A method called `get` makes later `@get(...)` decorators refer to it: use `from clientx import methods` and `@methods.get(...)` instead. A method called `list` (or `dict`, `type`, ...) makes a later `list[Post]`, in an annotation or a decorator argument, fail when the class is defined with `TypeError: 'function' object is not subscriptable` (pyright reports it too). Define that method last in the class, or write `builtins.list[Post]` after it (`import builtins`).
- Names `ClientX` itself uses can't be endpoint or resource names on a `ClientX` subclass: `user_agent`, `client`, and dunder methods raise `EndpointNameConflictError`. They're free on a `Resource`. `send` is free on both.
- mypy reports `empty-body` for `...` bodies with a non-`None` return type. Turn that code off for client modules (`# mypy: disable-error-code="empty-body"`); pyright accepts `...`.

Using clients:

- `ClientX(base_url, user_agent=None, raise_for_status=True, validate_arguments=False, **kwargs)` forwards every other keyword to `httpx2.Client`; `user_agent` wins over a `User-Agent` in `headers=`, and without either it's `ClientX/<version>`. The keywords include `auth`, `headers`, `params`, `cookies`, `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `proxy`, `transport`, `mounts`, `event_hooks`, `follow_redirects`, and so on. Use `with` to close connections. `client.client` is the underlying `httpx2.Client`, for ad-hoc requests.
- Status codes: a 4xx or 5xx response raises `httpx2.HTTPStatusError` from every endpoint, with the body already read (`exc.response.json()` works) and before any decoder runs. Redirects aren't errors: with `follow_redirects=True` only the final response is checked, and without it a 3xx is returned. A streamed error response is read and closed before raising. Turn it off for a client with `ClientX(..., raise_for_status=False)`, or per endpoint with `@get(..., raise_for_status=False)` (the endpoint's setting wins), for example to return a 404 as a `Response` or to let a decoder handle error statuses. Don't add a `raise_for_status` decoder or event hook.
- Argument validation is opt-in: `ClientX(..., validate_arguments=True)`, or `@get(..., validate_arguments=...)` per endpoint (the endpoint's setting wins). It checks each argument the caller passes against its full annotation (including `Field` constraints) in Pydantic's strict mode, before sending, and raises `ArgumentValidationError` (`.parameter`, `.validation_error`). Values are never converted (`"1"` doesn't match `int`), defaults aren't checked, and types Pydantic can't validate (such as `BinaryIO`) are skipped.
- Test clients with `transport=httpx2.MockTransport(handler)`, where `handler(request: httpx2.Request) -> httpx2.Response`.
- Errors all derive from `clientx.ClientXError`. When the class is defined: `MissingReturnTypeError`, `MissingDecoderError`, `EndpointNameConflictError`, `MissingPathArgumentsError` (a path or resource-prefix placeholder that names no parameter), `PathTemplateError` (a converter other than `{name:path}`), `EndpointSignatureError` (no positional first parameter for the client, or a `*args`/`**kwargs` parameter), and `MisplacedHelperError` (for a model field, when the class is defined if a parameter is annotated with the model, or else when it's sent). At call time: `UnconsumableArgumentError`, `PathValueError`, `UnboundResourceError`, and `ArgumentValidationError` when validation is on. Annotations are evaluated when the class is defined, so `from __future__ import annotations` works; types they name must be module-level. HTTP errors come from httpx2: connection errors, timeouts, and `HTTPStatusError` for 4xx and 5xx responses.
- Logging: one DEBUG record per endpoint call on the `clientx` logger, such as `ClientX request: GET /users/42 -> 200 in 12.3 ms (Users.retrieve)` (or `-> 404 HTTPStatusError`), with attributes `clientx_endpoint`, `clientx_method`, `clientx_path`, `clientx_parts`, `clientx_stream`, `clientx_status`, `clientx_elapsed_ms`, and `clientx_error`. It never contains header values, bodies, or query strings. httpx2 separately logs each request at INFO on the `httpx2` logger. For custom request logging, pass httpx2 `event_hooks`.
- To list a client's endpoints for docs or tooling, use `clientx.tools.list_tools(client)` (below): name, method, full path, tags, docstring and schemas, including resources. There's no global endpoint registry, and `Endpoint` isn't public.

AI tools and MCP:

- `clientx.tools.list_tools(client, read_only=False, include_tags=None, exclude_tags=(), include_deprecated=False)` returns one `Tool` per endpoint, including resources: `name` (attribute path with underscores, such as `users_retrieve`), `description` (the docstring), `input_schema` and `output_schema` (JSON Schema), `read_only` / `destructive` / `idempotent` (from the HTTP method: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are read-only; PUT, PATCH and DELETE are destructive; POST is neither and isn't idempotent; GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent), `method`, `path`, `tags`, and `deprecated`. `tool.call(arguments)` validates the arguments and calls the endpoint through the client, returning a JSON-friendly result; errors propagate, including `HTTPStatusError` for 4xx and 5xx responses (the MCP server turns them into error results with the status, method, path and start of the body, never the host or query string). An `HTTPStatusError`'s own message has the full URL, so don't send `str(error)` to a model if the client puts credentials in query parameters. `read_only=True` keeps only GET, HEAD and OPTIONS endpoints. Streaming endpoints are left out.
- `clientx.mcp.run_mcp_server(client, read_only=True)` serves those tools as an MCP server over stdio (it needs the `mcp` extra). `create_mcp_server(...)` returns the low-level `mcp.server.lowlevel.Server` for other transports. Don't print to stdout in an MCP server process.
- Docstrings become tool descriptions. Describe a parameter with the helper's `description=`: `Annotated[int | None, Query("userId", description="...")]`, or `Annotated[int, PathParam(description="...")]` for a path parameter (`PathParam` only describes; a `PathParam()` parameter without a placeholder in the path, prefix included, raises `EndpointSignatureError` when the class is defined, and `PathParam` on a model field raises `MisplacedHelperError`). A description goes into the parameter's or field's JSON Schema (so into tool and MCP schemas, and a model's `model_json_schema()`) and never changes the request. `pydantic.Field(description=...)` also works and wins if both are given. Keep credentials in the client's configuration (`auth=`, `headers=`), never in endpoint parameters, which models see and fill in.

## Docs

- [README](https://github.com/slatecipher/ClientX/blob/mainline/README.md): the full guide, covering endpoints, decoders, streaming, request payloads, resources, logging, AI tools, MCP, and errors
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/slatecipher/ClientX/blob/mainline/CHANGELOG.md): changes in each release; the API may change between minor versions before 1.0

## Examples

- [Beeceptor example client](https://github.com/slatecipher/ClientX/tree/mainline/examples/beeceptor): a complete client with resources, model decoders, and a deprecated endpoint, run by `examples/beeceptor_example.py`
- [JSONPlaceholder example client](https://github.com/slatecipher/ClientX/tree/mainline/examples/jsonplaceholder): a client for a real public API with the request-part helpers (`Query("userId")`, `Body` with `exclude_unset` for PATCH), camelCase aliases, and a 404 caught as `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`, run by `examples/jsonplaceholder_example.py` (it needs network access)
- [AI tools example](https://github.com/slatecipher/ClientX/blob/mainline/examples/beeceptor_tools_example.py): the same client's endpoints as AI tools, with definitions, schemas, filters, and calls
